name: Halo Effect
description: A positive impression of someone or something in one dimension (e.g. appearance) causes an unwarranted positive inference in unrelated dimensions (e.g. competence, trustworthiness).
design_relevance_note: The mechanism behind the Aesthetic-Usability Effect specifically, and more broadly cited to justify visual-polish investment as a proxy for trust signaling.
prevalence_note: Extremely widely known both within and outside design practice, one of the most mainstream named cognitive biases.

findings.description: Much of what looks like 'halo' bias in trait ratings can be predicted by ordinary linguistic similarity between the trait words themselves, not only by a psychological 'global impression' effect: cosine similarity between trait-name word embeddings predicted how likely people judged two traits to co-occur in a person, explaining up to 45% of the variance — even after confirming the trait-word pairs weren't simple synonyms.
findings.effect_size: cross-validated r² = .19 (lexical similarity alone) rising to .45 with additional word-similarity measures
findings.source_title: A Constant Error, Revisited: A New Explanation of the Halo Effect

findings.description: Ratings of the same person across distinct, ostensibly independent traits (intelligence, industry, technical skill, reliability) were highly and evenly correlated across raters — attributed to a general 'good or inferior' impression of the whole person contaminating judgment of each specific trait. A parallel WWI officer-rating example showed Intelligence correlating with Physique/Leadership/Character at .51-.64, far higher than genuinely independent traits should produce.
findings.source_title: A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings

applications.title: Asch's 1946 trait-order experiment: the same six traits, reordered, change the whole impression
applications.description: Solomon Asch presented participants with one of two lists of the same six personality traits ('intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious' vs. the reverse order), and found the list opening with positive traits produced a substantially more favorable overall impression of the person than the identical list opening with negative traits -- an early positive trait 'haloing' the interpretation of every trait that follows it.
applications.ethical_note: A controlled lab experiment on trait-order perception, not a designed influence on a user -- no persuasion or manipulation dimension to grade. Directly relevant to how UI copy, review summaries, or AI-generated profile descriptions order positive vs. negative information first, since this experiment shows that ordering alone measurably shifts perceived character.

applications.title: Cisco Systems: the same management and culture called 'flawless' in 1997 and 'a mess' by 2001
applications.description: As Cisco Systems' stock and reputation soared in the late 1990s, Wired described the company as filled with 'shiny, happy people' and BusinessWeek credited its success to CEO John Chambers' 'seemingly flawless management.' After the stock collapsed from $80 to $14 a share by 2001 and thousands were laid off, Fortune declared 'Cisco made its own mess,' blaming the very same management, acquisitions, and culture that had been praised as visionary just years earlier.
applications.ethical_note: A media-and-management case study, not a designed influence on a user -- directly relevant to how design and business teams cite 'what great companies do' case studies (Good to Great, In Search of Excellence, and similar bestsellers are named directly in Rosenzweig's critique): a company's specific practices are often retroactively labeled 'visionary' or 'flawed' based on how its stock performed, not independently assessed on their own merits.

applications.title: The Decision Lab's own login-page aesthetics experiment
applications.description: The Decision Lab ran a first-party controlled experiment presenting participants with one of two versions of a fictional app's login page, identical except for background color (bright yellow vs. pale yellow). Participants who liked the aesthetics of the page they saw rated the app's expected usability, reliability, and security substantially more favorably than participants who disliked the aesthetics -- despite the login page carrying no actual information about any of those attributes.
applications.industry_context: general software / product teams (research stimulus, not a real shipped app)
applications.ethical_note: A pure research demonstration of a perceptual bias with no persuasion or dark-pattern angle -- it measures how aesthetics affect trust perceptions, it doesn't itself manipulate users. Included because it's a genuine first-party experiment (unusual strength for this corpus's open-web-sourced Application layer) rather than third-party commentary about someone else's practice.
